fetched_contents.text: Suitability of leaching test methods for fly ash and slag: A review 1. Introduction Industrial solid waste leachate pollution is one of the important environmental problems the world faces today. It is an issue that adversely affects the society economically, physically and everyday life of people. The contamination of the water sources and soil due to industrial solid waste leachate is also being linked to some of the diseases that are around currently. It is reported that, frequent ingestion of chromium contaminated water can cause anemia and stomach cancer. Iron ingestion in large quantities results in a condition known as heamochromatosis, where in tissue damage results from iron accumulation (Indian Minerals Yearbook, 2012). In central India, Chhattisgarh is a potential power hub having sufficient mineral resources with surplus energy generation and the largest steel plant in India, which attracts and supports many industries. Natural resources such as water and land are limited and their per capita availability is actually diminishing because of irrational exploitation of natural coal and iron ore resources. The biggest challenge that Chhattisgarh faces is the degradation of environment and natural resources, which is imposing an alarming health hazard. Lack of efficient industrial solid wastes management, particularly in developing countries like India, has lead to severe environmental problems. Due to limited land for waste disposal, the current practice of uncontrolled dumping of fly ash near industrial belt of towns/cities has created a serious environmental problem due to leachate with presence of various toxic metal and ions (Nalawade, Bholay, & Mule, 2012). It is very important to know the characteristics of the surface water, rain water surrounding the waste disposal sites. The leachate immensely affects the sources of water near to dumpsites. (Singh et al., 2014). Leachate is the liquid produced when water percolate through any permeable material. It can contain either dissolved or suspended material, or usually both (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leachate). Leaching methods are categorized, often based on modes whether the leaching fluid is a single addition (static extraction tests), or is renewed (dynamic tests). Methods can also be classified as batch leaching, in which the sample is placed in a given volume of leachant solution, and as column or flow through systems, and as bulk or flow around systems for monolithic samples (Kim, 2005). Commonly used methods are developed by EPA or promulgated by ASTM. The Washington State Department of Ecology's (December 2003, Publication No. 03-09-107) report (available online at http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/tcp/cleanup.html) indicates that the leaching of contaminants from fill material is a complex process and that the use of leaching test to predict these processes is an evolving area of science. As such, no one single laboratory leaching test can evaluate the leaching behavior of a wide variety of material in a broad range of management scenarios. However, when used within the proper framework, leaching test can provide useful information for environmental decision-making. A thermal power plant generates large amounts of fly ash which may contain toxic metals and environmental risks associated with these coal fly ashes during wet storage in the ash ponds (Lokeshappa, Dikshit, Giammar, Luo, & Catalano, 2010). The disposal of coal fly ash subjects these metal rich materials to conditions that result in further sequestration of the metals or to their release to the environment (Lokeshappa & Dikshit, 2011). The release and transport of trace metals from coal fly ash material is an area of environmental concern because of the wet storage in the ash ponds. The volatilization, melting, decomposition and the formation of new materials and oxidation are the main mechanisms to transfer the metals from coal to fly ash (Kim, Kazonich, & Dahlberg, 2003). The major potential impacts of fly ash disposal either in ash pond or reused in the cement industry leads to leaching of potentially toxic substances into soils, surface water and groundwater. Environmental concerns regarding the potential contamination of soil, surface and groundwater due to the presence of soluble metal species in the ash pond leachate are of great concern (Praharaj, Powell, Hart, & Tripathy, 2002). The soluble salt content in ashes is closely related to the coal properties and the age of the fly ash and also to the pH and other environmental conditions (Jankowski, Ward, French, Groves, 2006). With respect to leaching, it is important to recognize that coal utilized by products, particularly fly ash, is not a homogenous material. Its elemental and mineralogical composition and its physical properties are a function of the original coal, the combustion temperature and post-combustion cooling rate (Kim, 2002). Volatilization, melting, decomposition, and the formation of new minerals, as well as oxidation, are the mechanisms that transform the minerals in coal (Ann G. Kim). 1.1. Leaching test methods In general, leaching tests can be classified into the following categories (Environment Canada, 1990): (a) tests designed to simulate contaminant release under a specific environmental scenario (e.g., synthetic acid rain leach test or TCLP), (b) sequential chemical extraction tests, or (c) tests which assess fundamental leaching parameters. Many researchers have tried to simulate real-life scenario and suggested various leaching methods justifying the attempts. According to Kosson, van der Sloot, Sanchezand, and Garrabrants (2002) the tests that are designed to simulate release under specific environmental scenarios are limited because they most often do not provide information on release under environmental scenarios different from the one being simulated. fetched_contents.text: Distributions and Leaching Behaviors of Toxic Elements in Fly Ash Abstract Fly ash usually contains a considerable amount of toxic elements that can be leached into the environment, thereby easily leading to serious contaminations. In this work, the leaching behaviors of poisonous elements including boron (B), phosphorus (P), vanadium (V), chromium (Cr), arsenic (As), selenium (Se), molybdenum (Mo), antimony (Sb), and tungsten (W) from fly ash were explored by sequential extraction. Importantly, the associations of these elements in fly ash were discussed based on their leaching and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) results. From the XANES results, it was observed that V(IV), Cr(III), As(V), Se(IV), and W(IV) were their main states of existence in fly ash. In terms of leaching results, large amounts of Mo and W were leached into pure water, which indicated their high mobilities. Furthermore, the occurrence of Mo in fly ash was mainly in the form of oxides, and W had complex associations including WX4 (X can be monovalent anions), its reduction state or association with the elements that can be oxidized, and existence in silicates. B was as easily released into the environment as Mo and W. It can have several associations with the other cations, such as Ca2+, Na+, and Mg2+, and occurs in silicates. In contrast, most of the Cr and Sb were locked in silicates, indicating that they were very stable in fly ash. In addition, P, V, and As can exist within the structure of silicates as well. However, a considerable amount of them leached in the reduction step with a low pH. Hence, they can be associated with Ca2+, Na+, Mg2+, or Fe3+. In terms of Se, oxidation processes played an important role in controlling its leaching because of the oxidation of Se(IV) to Se(VI). Calcium selenite should be the predominant form of Se in fly ash. 1. Introduction Coal as an energy source for power generation has been used for a long time. Every year, billions of tons of coal are burnt, which, meanwhile, generates large amounts of fly ash that is regarded as an industrial waste.1 If it cannot be disposed off properly, serious environmental problems, such as water and soil contamination and disruption of ecological cycles, would be easily caused. Many aggressive efforts have been carried out toward recycling the fly ash for utilization.2 In addition to being used as an additive in cement, fly ash has been used in many other applications, including road base construction, soil amendment, and zeolite and geopolymer synthesis. However, these applications are not sufficient for the complete utilization of the generated fly ash. There is still a great deal of fly ash disposed in ash ponds, lagoons, or landfills.2 The main harmful aspect of the fly ash during its utilization or disposal is that the toxic elements in the fly ash are likely to be released into the environment when it comes in contact with water. It has been reported that the trace element concentrations in fly ash are generally 4–10 times higher than their original concentrations in coal.3 Among the toxic elements in fly ash, the metalloid elements are usually present in anionic forms in solution. Some metal elements, such as vanadium (V), molybdenum (Mo), and tungsten (W), can also exist in the form of anions in aqueous condition. Because of the negative charge of these ions, they exhibit a higher mobility, which means that they can lead to environmental pollution and human health problems broadly and extensively. Thus, more attention should be paid to the control of anionic pollutants possibly leached from the fly ash; this is imperative for a better understanding of the occurrences of these elements in fly ash. The possible chemical associations of the trace elements in fly ash have also been noted. Finkelman et al.4 proposed that arsenic (As) was primarily associated with pyrite in coals, which later was decomposed during burning and gave rise to a dominant surface association in fly ash. This was also confirmed by Goodarzi and Huggins.5,6 Being similar to As, boron (B) and Mo are also recognized as surface associations, which means that they can be easily released from fly ash. Sulfur (S) is a major soluble element in fly ash in the form of SO42– that has a strong relationship with calcium (Ca) leaching. Selenium (Se) is an element that is most strongly enriched in coal with respect to many rocks, and coal fly ash can be viewed as a major source of this element.7,8 A view that the Se species can also be in the structure of calcium sulfide was proposed by Freyer and Voigt.9 Other elements including chromium (Cr), antimony (Sb), and V are deemed to be associated with the aluminosilicates (primarily in glass phase) in fly ash.5,10,11 However, Hansen’s research implied that V and Sb were associated with the surface materials on the ash particles.12 Phosphorus (P) was believed to be extremely insoluble in fly ash,13 but there are very limited data available in the literature supporting this viewpoint.14 In terms of W, Vassilev and Vassileva15 detected soluble scheelite in coal fly ash, and until now, there was no other report on the occurrence of W in fly ash. Therefore, even though the research on chemical associations of trace elements in fly ash has been considerable, the distributions of these elements in fly ash have not been understood comprehensively. There are still contradictions in terms of the existing states of some elements in fly ash. Thus, in this investigation, a modified sequential extraction procedure was adopted to explore the occurrences of elements including B, P, V, Cr, As, Se, Mo, Sb, and W in fly ash. X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) was applied to determine the valences of specific elements by comparing with reference materials. Leaching test results from different countries show that metal mobility in coal fly ash is highly context-dependent, with test methods, sample preparation, and leaching conditions shaping the measured concentrations and mobility patterns. The evidence suggests that countries and regions use a range of standardized protocols, including EPA-, ASTM-, and national methods, and that leaching behavior is often analyzed for a broad set of metals rather than a narrow subset [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5].

The metals and conditions typically measured across the evidence span toxic elements such as chromium (Cr), arsenic (As), selenium (Se), vanadium (V), molybdenum (Mo), tungsten (W), antimony (Sb), boron (B), phosphorus (P), and cadmium (Cd), among others [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The evidence also notes that some studies explicitly compare leaching behaviors under different leaching procedures, such as acid leaching, wet oxidation, and sequential extraction, and that leachates are analyzed for 30 elements in one case [N2-R4][N2-R5][N1-R5]. This implies that test protocols are not uniform across countries, and the metals measured often reflect the specific environmental concerns and regulatory priorities of the region.

Leaching concentrations vary across countries and test protocols because the behavior of metals is influenced by ash composition, pH, sample preparation, and leaching conditions. The review material notes that coal fly ash is not homogeneous and that its elemental and mineralogical composition depends on the original coal, combustion temperature, and post-combustion cooling rate [N1-F1]. It also highlights that soluble salts, pH, and environmental conditions are closely related to ash characteristics, and that leaching methods can be classified as static extraction tests, dynamic tests, batch leaching, column tests, or bulk tests [N1-F1]. The comparative leaching study further shows that some metals, such as Mo and W, are highly mobile in pure water, while Cr and Sb are more stable in silicates [N2-F2]. This variation explains why concentrations can differ across studies: Mo and W may appear more leachable in acidic or water-based tests, whereas Cr and Sb may remain largely bound under similar conditions [N2-F2][N1-F1].

The evidence also suggests that results can be inconsistent across test protocols because different methods simulate different environmental scenarios and may not capture the same leaching behavior. The review states that tests designed to simulate release under specific scenarios often do not provide information on release under different scenarios, and that reliance on simulation-based methods can lead to misuse and misinterpretation [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence from a comparative leaching study shows that sequential extraction and XANES-based analysis can reveal different associations and mobility states for the same elements, indicating that leaching behavior depends on both test design and sample mineralogy [N2-F2]. Overall, the country-specific test results support a picture of metal mobility that is inconsistent when protocols differ, because methods, leachants, duration, and ash properties all affect the outcome [N1-F1][N2-F2][N2-R4].

Environmental safety criteria support or weaken the conclusion that heavy metals in coal fly ash are environmentally safe depending on how thresholds are defined, how leaching results compare to those thresholds, and which endpoints are considered in safety judgments. The evidence indicates that safety is judged against drinking water standards, soil thresholds, and leaching limits, with EPA and EU thresholds appearing as important reference points [N3-R1][N3-F3].

The concentration thresholds used to judge safety are not universally identical across endpoints. The evidence provides EPA drinking water standards for a range of heavy metals, including antimony (0.006 mg/L), arsenic (0.010 mg/L), cadmium (0.005 mg/L), chromium (0.1 mg/L), copper (1.3 mg/L), and lead (0.010 mg/L), among others [N3-F3]. It also notes that soil permissible limits differ by metal and jurisdiction, with the EU, WHO, and US EPA thresholds used in one source, and Cu limits in soil ranging from 50 to 140 mg/kg [N3-R1][N3-R5]. These thresholds are important because they define what is considered “safe” in water versus soil, and they vary by metal and endpoint.

Leaching results in the evidence are mixed relative to these thresholds. Some studies show that certain metals are highly mobile, such as Mo and W, which can leach into pure water in large amounts [N2-F2]. This directly challenges a broad conclusion of safety, because even if concentrations are below a threshold in one study, mobility can still pose risk if leaching conditions in the real world approach or exceed those thresholds [N2-F2]. At the same time, the evidence also shows that some metals are more stable: Cr and Sb are locked in silicates, and P, V, and As can be associated with Ca²+, Na⁺, Mg²+, or Fe³+ under certain conditions [N2-F2]. This suggests that leaching results can sometimes fall below safety thresholds, but only under specific test conditions rather than in all contexts.

The endpoints considered in safety judgments are soil, water, and groundwater. The review explicitly notes that leachate can affect soil, surface water, and groundwater, and that the main concern is contamination of these media through soluble metal species [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The EPA drinking water regulations also clearly target water systems, including drinking water standards and treatment techniques [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a multi-endpoint view of safety: a metal may be within water standards, yet still pose soil or groundwater risk if it leaches into those media [N3-R1][N3-F3][N2-F2]. In this sense, the safety criteria both support and weaken the conclusion. They provide a concrete benchmark for judging risk, but they also reveal that mobility in one endpoint does not guarantee safety in another [N3-R1][N3-F3][N2-F2].

Leaching tests may or may not support a broad conclusion of environmental safety because of important assumptions, uncertainties, and limitations in how the tests are designed and interpreted. The evidence shows that leaching tests are used to assess contaminant release under specific environmental scenarios, but they are not perfect predictors of real-world conditions [N1-F1]. One review explicitly states that tests designed to simulate release under specific scenarios often do not provide information on release under different scenarios, and that reliance on such methods can lead to misuse and misinterpretation [N1-F1]. This is a major reason why leaching results should not be taken as definitive proof of environmental safety.

Test design, duration, and sample preparation affect conclusions in several ways. The evidence mentions that leaching methods can be static extraction tests, dynamic tests, batch leaching, column tests, or bulk tests, and that the choice of method can alter the outcome [N1-F1]. The comparative leaching study also shows that sequential extraction and XANES-based analysis can reveal different associations and mobility states for the same elements, indicating that test design shapes the interpretation of mobility [N2-F2]. Furthermore, the evidence notes that leaching behavior can depend on the pH, soluble salt content, and other environmental conditions, and that coal fly ash is not homogeneous [N1-F1]. This means that short-term batch tests may not capture long-term behavior, and that sample preparation can change the apparent leachability of metals [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Site-specific factors and long-term behavior further complicate the extrapolation from laboratory tests to the real world. The evidence indicates that leaching is a complex process, and that the use of leaching tests to predict leaching behavior in a broad range of management scenarios is an evolving science [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that coal fly ash is subject to conditions that may result in further sequestration of metals or their release to the environment, and that wet storage in ash ponds can increase the risk of trace-metal release [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Long-term behavior matters because metals can migrate over time, especially under variable moisture, temperature, and geochemical conditions, and because stabilization or mobilization can occur in ways not captured by short-term tests [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Taken together, these points show that leaching tests are useful for environmental decision-making, but they are not sufficient on their own to support a broad conclusion of safety [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Regulatory acceptance of coal fly ash does not necessarily prove environmental safety because regulatory classification differs from actual toxicity or leaching risk. The evidence shows that some regulatory contexts treat coal fly ash as non-hazardous or non-regulated, even though the material can contain toxic elements that may leach under certain conditions [N5-R2][N6-R5]. A review also notes that coal fly ash and other coal combustion wastes have not been listed as hazardous materials in some jurisdictions, and that this non-hazardous status is a legal classification rather than an assurance of safety [N5-R2]. This distinction is important: legal exemption or non-hazardous status does not automatically mean the material is harmless; it means the regulatory system has not classified it as requiring the same controls as hazardous wastes [N5-R2][N6-R5].

Legal exemptions or non-hazardous status imply about safety that they reflect regulatory priorities and risk-management trade-offs, not an absence of risk. The evidence indicates that EPA removed regulations on coal fly ash as special hazardous wastes in 1980, and that some jurisdictions still do not regulate coal fly ash as hazardous materials [N6-R3][N5-R2]. At the same time, the same evidence also notes that the EPA has found that living next to a coal ash disposal site can increase cancer or other disease risks, and that coal ash may emit toxics into air under certain conditions [N4-R5][N4-R3]. This shows that regulatory acceptance can coexist with environmental risk, because regulation is often based on available knowledge, exposure pathways, and cost-benefit considerations rather than complete elimination of hazard [N4-R5][N4-R3][N6-R5].

Management practices can reduce risk even if tests are inconclusive, which is one reason regulatory acceptance can still be meaningful. The evidence points to beneficial use, beneficial-user guidelines, and case studies of stabilization projects, including pond excavation and landfill operations [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. These practices can limit exposure by encapsulating fly ash, controlling moisture, reducing direct contact with water, and managing disposal sites in ways that lower the likelihood of leaching [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The review also emphasizes that increased public awareness and better disposal and management are central to addressing toxicity concerns [N5-R1]. So, regulatory acceptance can support environmental safety if it is accompanied by effective management, but it cannot substitute for a rigorous assessment of actual toxicity and leaching risk [N5-R1][N5-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Instead, the results indicate that metal mobility is highly context-dependent, and that safety depends on thresholds, endpoints, regulatory classification, and management practices. In other words, the tests can be useful for environmental decision-making, but they are not sufficient on their own to justify a general conclusion of safety [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-R2].

### 1) What the leaching test results show about metal mobility

The branch report on country-specific leaching tests shows that metal mobility varies by test method, sample preparation, and leaching conditions [N1-F1]. Some studies also explicitly compare leaching behaviors under different procedures, such as acid leaching, wet oxidation, and sequential extraction [N2-R4][N2-R5].

The comparative leaching results show that concentrations vary because ash composition, pH, and environmental conditions affect leaching behavior. The review material notes that coal fly ash is not homogeneous and that its elemental and mineralogical composition depends on the original coal, combustion temperature, and post-combustion cooling rate [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that soluble salts, pH, and environmental conditions are closely related to ash characteristics, and that leaching methods can be classified as static extraction tests, dynamic tests, batch leaching, column tests, or bulk tests [N1-F1]. The comparative leaching study further shows that some metals, such as Mo and W, are highly mobile in pure water, whereas Cr and Sb are more stable in silicates [N2-F2].

This matters for interpretation: leaching results can be inconsistent across test protocols because different methods simulate different environmental scenarios and may not capture the same leaching behavior [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that sequential extraction and XANES-based analysis can reveal different associations and mobility states for the same elements, reinforcing that test design shapes the outcome [N2-F2]. So the branch report’s bottom line is that leaching results are context-sensitive and can point to highly variable mobility patterns [N1-F1][N2-F2].

These practices can limit exposure by encapsulating fly ash, controlling moisture, reducing direct contact with water, and managing disposal sites in ways that lower the likelihood of leaching [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The review also emphasizes that increased public awareness and better disposal and management are central to addressing toxicity concerns [N5-R1]. So regulatory acceptance can support environmental safety if it is accompanied by effective management, but it cannot substitute for a rigorous assessment of actual toxicity and leaching risk [N5-R1][N5-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 4) Why leaching tests may or may not support a broad conclusion of safety

Leaching tests may not support a broad conclusion of safety because they are limited by assumptions, uncertainties, and site-specific conditions. The evidence shows that leaching tests are used to assess contaminant release under specific environmental scenarios, but they are not perfect predictors of real-world conditions [N1-F1]. One review explicitly states that tests designed to simulate release under specific scenarios often do not provide information on release under different scenarios, and that reliance on such methods can lead to misuse and misinterpretation [N1-F1]. This is a major reason why leaching results should not be taken as definitive proof of environmental safety.

Test design, duration, and sample preparation affect conclusions in several ways. The evidence mentions that leaching methods can be static extraction tests, dynamic tests, batch leaching, column tests, or bulk tests, and that the choice of method can alter the outcome [N1-F1]. The comparative leaching study also shows that sequential extraction and XANES-based analysis can reveal different associations and mobility states for the same elements, indicating that test design shapes the interpretation of mobility [N2-F2]. Furthermore, the evidence notes that leaching behavior can depend on the pH, soluble salt content, and other environmental conditions, and that coal fly ash is not homogeneous [N1-F1]. This means that short-term batch tests may not capture long-term behavior, and that sample preparation can change the apparent leachability of metals [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Site-specific factors and long-term behavior further complicate the extrapolation from laboratory tests to the real world. The evidence indicates that leaching is a complex process, and that the use of leaching tests to predict leaching behavior in a broad range of management scenarios is an evolving science [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that coal fly ash is subject to conditions that may result in further sequestration of metals or their release to the environment, and that wet storage in ash ponds can increase the risk of trace-metal release [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Long-term behavior matters because metals can migrate over time, especially under variable moisture, temperature, and geochemical conditions, and because stabilization or mobilization can occur in ways not captured by short-term tests [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Taken together, these points show that leaching tests are useful for environmental decision-making, but they are not sufficient on their own to support a broad conclusion of safety [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the leaching test results from different countries do **not** strongly support a broad conclusion that heavy metals in coal fly ash are environmentally safe. They show that metal mobility is highly context-dependent, and that leaching concentrations vary across countries and test protocols because of differences in methods, sample preparation, and environmental conditions [N1-F1][N2-F2]. At the same time, safety criteria provide important thresholds, but they are endpoint-specific and do not automatically validate safety across all media and conditions [N3-R1][N3-F3][N2-F2].

Regulatory acceptance also does not prove safety. Non-hazardous or non-regulated status is a legal classification, not a guarantee that the material is harmless [N5-R2][N6-R5]. Management practices can reduce risk, but they do not eliminate it entirely [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. Finally, leaching tests themselves are limited by assumptions, uncertainties, and site-specific factors, so they should be treated as useful but incomplete tools for environmental decision-making [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Bottom line
The evidence supports a cautious conclusion: **leaching test results can suggest some metals are relatively stable under specific conditions, but they do not establish that all heavy metals in coal fly ash are environmentally safe.** A safer interpretation is that the tests are informative, not conclusive, and that environmental safety depends on thresholds, multiple endpoints, regulatory context, and management practices [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-R2][N6-R5].
